entries.claim: Dispersion of any set of values means divergence, or the differences between its values.

entries.note: Definition clearly shown in pink box, though using 'divergent' rather than 'divergence'

entries.claim: The dispersion is small if the differences between the values are little, whereas the dispersion is great if the differences between the values are very big.
entries.quote: The dispersion is small if the difference between the values are little
entries.note: Both parts of the rule (small/great) fully stated in pink box

entries.claim: When the dispersion is zero, all the values are equal.

entries.claim: The dispersion is a measure that expresses how homogeneous the sets are.
entries.quote: the dispersion is a measure that express how much the sets are homogenous

entries.claim: The range is the difference between the greatest value and the smallest value in the set.
entries.quote: It is the diference between the greatest value and the smallest value in the set.

entries.claim: (1) The range is the simplest and easiest method of measuring dispersion.
entries.quote: The range is the simplest and easiest method of measuring dispersion.

entries.claim: (2) The range is influenced greatly by the outlier. The values of the second set disperse in a range of 50; when the last value (92) is removed the range = 52 - 42 = 10, or 1/5 of the previous range.
entries.quote: The range is influenced greatly by the outlier.
entries.note: All claim elements present in 'Notice that:' point (2)

entries.claim: (3) The range is not influenced by any value in the set except the greatest and smallest values, so it does not give a clear picture of the dispersion of the set.
entries.quote: Since the range doesn't influence by any value in the set
